NOVELTY STATEMENT (INTERVENTION)
The proposed intervention is a closed-loop, feedforward temperature setpoint retuning procedure that dynamically lowers the reactor inlet temperature during low steam-to-hydrocarbon (S/HC) ratio transients to suppress the thermodynamic driving force for coke formation, while maintaining the temperature high enough to sustain styrene yield. Standard practice uses a fixed temperature setpoint optimized for nominal steam rates, assuming steady-state operation; this creates a mismatch where the catalyst operates at a higher effective severity during steam turndown or feed fluctuations, accelerating deactivation. The adjacent-technique clearance is that while adaptive control is common in chemical plants, applying a specific inverse-relationship temperature correction strictly to compensate for S/HC ratio deviations in a fixed-bed styrene reactor is a distinct procedural configuration change not typically hard-coded in standard steady-state optimization. The mechanism attacks the failure's driving physics by reducing the local hydrocarbon partial pressure and the thermal energy available for pyrolytic condensation reactions that form coke precursors, thereby lowering the coke formation rate integral over the duty cycle.

PHYSICS CHECK
DIRECTION-OF-EFFECT: driving variable = local temperature at the catalyst bed interface; the mechanism moves it DOWN (via setpoint retuning) by up to 20–30 K during low S/HC ratio conditions; this REDUCES the coke formation rate constant. The governing relation for coke deposition in styrene dehydrogenation is often approximated by an Arrhenius-type dependence on temperature, $k_{coke} \propto \exp(-E_a/RT)$. For a typical coke activation energy $E_a \approx 80\text{ kJ/mol}$, a reduction in temperature $\Delta T = -20$ K at $T \approx 873$ K results in a ratio of $k_{new}/k_{old} = \exp(-E_a/R (1/T_{new} - 1/T_{old})) \approx 0.7$. This 30% reduction in the coke formation rate directly reduces the deactivation integral over the cycle, extending catalyst life. This direction is correct because higher temperatures accelerate secondary condensation reactions that form coke on the iron-potassium catalyst surface.

IMPLEMENTATION BILL
MECHANISM CLASS: Dynamic Setpoint Retuning Procedure

(a) Existing Flow Rate Transducers (FT): Used as-is to measure steam and hydrocarbon flow rates. No hardware change.
(a) Existing Pressure Transducers (PT): Used as-is to infer pressure drop and confirm bed integrity. No hardware change.
(c) Control System Logic Update: Implement a function block in the existing DCS that calculates the S/HC ratio in real-time. If $S/HC < 1.5$ (nominal), the target temperature setpoint is reduced by a calibrated factor (e.g., 15 K per 0.1 unit drop in S/HC). This is a procedural/configuration change to the existing control loop, no new hardware.
(c) Operator Procedure: Mandate that the automatic setpoint retuning is active during all batch cycles and that operators do not override the temperature setpoint manually unless safety interlocks trigger. This is a standard operational procedure update.

BURDEN LEDGER (STANDARD-PRACTICE PARITY)
Standard Practice Bill: Fixed temperature setpoint (e.g., 600°C), constant S/HC ratio target (e.g., 1.5). Burden: Zero dynamic control complexity, lower risk of over-heating during transients.
Intervention Bill: Dynamic temperature setpoint via DCS logic. Burden: Minor engineering time to code the function block in the existing DCS (no new hardware procurement). Operational Loss: Zero loss in energy or availability; the temperature reduction is within the safe operating envelope and actually reduces the risk of hot-spot excursion. The cost is a potential slight decrease in styrene yield per pass at the lower temperature, which is a standard trade-off for catalyst longevity. This is priced as a negative operational loss (i.e., yield loss) of approx. 0.5-1% during transient periods, which is net positive when offset by extended catalyst life and reduced replacement costs. Parity is concluded as SAME OR LOWER burden because no new hardware is added, only configuration changes to existing equipment.
EXECUTABLE TEST
Protocol: Run a 48-hour test campaign with two scenarios. Scenario A: Fixed temperature setpoint at 600°C with S/HC ratio modulated between 1.0 and 2.0. Scenario B: Dynamic setpoint retuning activated (temperature drops to 580°C when S/HC is 1.0, rises to 600°C when S/HC is 2.0). Measure the rate of pressure drop increase (proxy for coke deposition) and the styrene yield in both scenarios. Pass/Fail Threshold: Scenario B must show a pressure drop increase rate at least 20% lower than Scenario A, with a yield penalty of less than 1%. Duration: 48 hours to observe cumulative effects. Kill Criterion: If Scenario B shows a yield penalty greater than 5% or if the pressure drop rate does not decrease, the mechanism is ineffective and must be discarded.

CONSTRAINT-BIND / RISK
The constraint allows "temperature setpoint retuning" or "load-ramp procedure". This mechanism uses temperature setpoint retuning. The constraint also allows "steam-to-hydrocarbon ratio procedure". This mechanism uses the S/HC ratio as a signal to drive the temperature retuning. No new hardware is installed, adhering to the permitted set. The risk is that the DCS function block implementation may be complex for the plant's engineering team, but it is within standard practice for modern control systems. No new instrumentation is added. The mechanism relies on existing FT and PT signals, which are stated to exist in the problem infrastructure.
